pr_title: Avoid a list/array allocation in Task.WhenAll(enumerable)
pr_body:
When the incoming enumerable isn't a `Task[]` or `List<Task>`, we end up allocating either a `Task[]` or a `List<T>` (which then may incur one or more array allocations under the covers). We can avoid that by using an internal builder.

Closes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/110530

issue_context.title: Possible Task.WhenAll performance improvements
issue_context.body:
Let me share a couple of considerations related to `Task.WhenAll` performance, specifically for `WhenAll<TResult>(IEnumerable<Task<TResult>> tasks)` overload.

1. Currently if `tasks` is not `ICollection<T>` and therefore the count is not known, it will create a list of tasks and then return `new WhenAllPromise<TResult>(list.ToArray())`. It seems like `WhenAllPromise` could take a `Span<T>` instead of an array, but currently it cannot because it stores that array into the field. Looks like the field is there only to be used in `ShouldNotifyDebuggerOfWaitCompletion` property and is probably needed only for debugging, can that allocation made by `list.ToArray()` be avoided in release builds?

2. I believe that it's pretty common when a set of tasks is produced for some collection of items, e.g when calling `source.Select(x => ProcessAsync(x))`. We know collection size, but then we're losing it when calling `Select`. It probably would make sense to handle `Iterator<T>` internal type to get task count if it's available to avoid unnecessary allocations.
comments:
> Looks like the field is there only to be used in ShouldNotifyDebuggerOfWaitCompletion property and is probably needed only for debugging, can that allocation made by list.ToArray() be avoided in release builds?

That's not the only reason it's there. It's used in Invoke, when the last constituent task completes, to extract the results/exceptions/etc. from all of the tasks, and importantly in the same order those tasks were provided.

> It probably would make sense to handle Iterator<T> internal type to get task count if it's available to avoid unnecessary allocations.

Task is in corelib. The `Iterator<T>` you mention is an internal implementation detail of System.Linq. There's no good way for `Task.WhenAll` to query the underlying type here to extract length details. It _could_ use something like the internal ValueListBuilder to at least use some stack memory / pooled memory as part of building up the temporary list.
@stephentoub does `Task.WhenEach` suffer from similar issues or is this 100% limited to `Task.WhenAll`?

> [@stephentoub](https://github.com/stephentoub) does `Task.WhenEach` suffer from similar issues or is this 100% limited to `Task.WhenAll`?

There's no "suffering" here :) My PR is a minor tweak to possibly avoid an allocation in the case where the incoming enumerable isn't a list/array.

Task.WhenEach is completely different. What are your concerns there?

To clarify, I wasn't necessarily referring to your PR, but to the overall topic here. And I guess the wording was not great on my part: consider it "caracteristics" instead of "issues" 😝

> Task.WhenEach is completely different. What are your concerns there?

It was just a question for my own understanding here. For new code, I suspect we'll end up using `WhenEach` substantially more over `WhenAll` and was wondering if there is a memory consideration there as well. I _assume_ that since `WhenEach` is lazily evaluated, it wouldn't have to preallocate an array like `WhenAll` is doing as per the OP?

> That's not the only reason it's there. It's used in Invoke, when the last constituent task completes, to extract the results/exceptions/etc. from all of the tasks, and importantly in the same order those tasks were provided.

It seems that `Invoke` is called only from the constructor and just iterates through the array, I was just wondering if the constructor could take a `Span` and hand it over to `Invoke`.

> Task is in corelib. The `Iterator<T>` you mention is an internal implementation detail of System.Linq.

Ah, it's in a different assembly, missed that.

> It seems that Invoke is called only from the constructor

That is not the case. `Invoke` provides the implementation of `ITaskCompletionAction.Invoke`, which is called when the task completes.

@stephentoub Got it, thanks.
Anyway, there will be an improvement in the core libraries, turns out it was worth starting a conversation :)

@stephentoub btw, what about `Memory<T>`? Though it has to be stored on the heap as well, would it be cheaper to use instead of allocating a new array with `ToArray`? (not sure if there's a way to get `Memory<T>` similar to `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan`).

> [@stephentoub](https://github.com/stephentoub) btw, what about `Memory<T>`? Though it has to be stored on the heap as well, would it be cheaper to use instead of allocating a new array with `ToArray`? (not sure if there's a way to get `Memory<T>` similar to `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan`).

> `Memory<T>` still needs to reference storage.

I mean it first creates a `List<T>` and then calls `ToArray`, would it be cheaper to use `Memory<T>` for its backing array instead?

review_comments:
The syntax for initializing the ValueListBuilder with an array is incorrect. The correct syntax should be `new ValueListBuilder<Task>(stackalloc Task[8]);`.
```suggestion
                new ValueListBuilder<Task>(stackalloc Task[8]);
```
